hints: Look at how each of the four statements combines the words magnitude and direction with the words scalar and vector.
Recall that magnitude means size or amount, for example $20 \text{ m}$ of distance, while direction means which way, for example east.
Test each statement against the rule that a scalar needs only magnitude whereas a vector needs both magnitude and direction.
walkthrough: Identify what is being tested: the precise meaning of magnitude and direction for scalar and vector quantities.
State the governing rule: a scalar quantity is fully specified by magnitude alone with no direction, while a vector quantity requires both magnitude and direction.
Link to examples: mass of $5 \text{ kg}$ needs no direction, but velocity of $10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ east needs both size and direction.

Check the cause-and-effect chain: the statement claiming a scalar has direction but not magnitude swaps the properties, and the statements claiming a vector has only one of magnitude or direction omit an essential property.
Only the statement that a scalar quantity has magnitude but not direction matches the definition exactly. This is option B

options.A: A scalar is described by magnitude alone, so giving it direction but no magnitude reverses the definition.
options.B: A scalar such as mass or temperature is fully specified by its magnitude with no direction.
options.C: A vector needs both magnitude and direction, so direction alone is incomplete.
options.D: Magnitude alone describes a scalar, whereas a vector must also have direction.
